title: How does a toilet flush without electricity?

sources.name: US EPA — Gravity and pressure-assisted flushing

practice: Enjoy another small mystery? Try the Science Quiz.

sections.html:
A gravity-flush toilet uses water stored above the bowl. Open a valve, and gravity sends that water down in a rush. The flush itself needs no electric motor.

You tap a lever, hear a swoosh, and the bowl empties. The quiet hero is the cistern: the tank behind the seat. It holds water until you ask for it.

The US Environmental Protection Agency describes gravity flushing as the work of stored water and its weight. Think of tipping a jug: raising the water first gives it somewhere to fall.
sections.title: The water is already waiting

sections.html:
In a siphonic toilet, the rushing water fills a curved passage behind the bowl. A siphon is a flow that carries water through a filled pipe and down to a lower outlet.

Once that flow starts, it draws water and waste out of the bowl. Air eventually enters the passage and breaks the siphon, ending the rush. Kohler follows this sequence in its explanation of a toilet flush.

That explains the sudden change in sound: a strong flow, then a gulp as the water and air change places.
sections.title: A hidden bend does the next job

sections.html:
The falling water level lowers a float inside the cistern. This floating part controls the fill valve, which lets fresh water in.

As the tank fills, the float rises. At the set level, it shuts the valve. The bowl also gets fresh water. These simple movements prepare the next flush without a timer or a computer.
sections.title: A little float gets it ready again

sections.html:
This is one common design. EPA distinguishes gravity flushing from pressure-assisted flushing, which uses water held under pressure. Some toilets use electric pumps, so the answer depends on the model.

Even a gravity toilet needs its water supply to refill. A motor-free flush is only one part of the whole plumbing system.

Good design can also use less water: EPA explains how efficient toilets are tested for both flushing performance and water use. The clever bit is making a carefully timed rush do a useful job.

For another familiar object with a clever job, explore how everyday things work.
sections.title: Does every toilet work this way?

description: A lever, a rush of water and a tiny float do a surprisingly clever job. Follow what happens inside an ordinary gravity-flush toilet.
